articles.title: EFF Celebrates Appeals Court Rejecting Expansive Copyright Claim
articles.content: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit handed internet users and programmers a big win today, by rejecting an attempt to stretch a narrow provision of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) into a new source of copyright liability. The case involves Section 1202 of the DMCA, which prohibits intentionally removing copyright management information (CMI) like an author’s name or a copyright notice, from a copyrighted work. Open AI and Microsoft used code from Github as part of the training data for their LLMs, along with billions of other works. A group of anonymous Github contributors sued, alleging the new code coming out of these LLMs was similar to theirs—but with the CMI stripped out. The Ninth Circuit correctly agreed with what we said in our brief : removing copyright information from a copyrighted work is fundamentally different from creating a new work that didn't have CMI in the first place. Section 1202 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act was intended to serve as a backstop for traditional copyrights in the digital age—not to create a new, more expansive right to inhibit otherwise non-infringing uses. As we also explained, accepting the Does’ theory would have created a brand-new source of liability for otherwise perfectly lawful activities, undermining creativity and innovation far beyond the specific context of AI development. Copyright holders would be able to file costly lawsuits against all kinds of legitimate users, such as artists making remixes based on older works, teachers adapting works for a classroom presentation, engineers reverse engineering code to understand it better, and search engines that help us all navigate the web. The risks would have fallen especially hard on independent software developers and other small creators. Large companies can afford to litigate these claims in federal court for years, if necessary. But an independent programmer facing massive statutory damages may simply have to settle, even when their underlying use is completely lawful. That’s why EFF fights to make sure courts don’t expand copyright beyond what Congress authorized. Copyright law still protects programmers when their work is unlawfully copied. They can still bring copyright infringement claims if someone uses a model to reproduce their code. Additionally, the plaintiffs’ contract claims against the AI companies are still in play. The specific holding here was narrow but important: that the absence of copyright information from a new work does not mean, by itself, that someone illegally removed it. That’s the correct result. New technologies will keep raising hard questions about copyright. Courts should answer those questions by applying the rights that Congress actually authorized, not by inventing new rights that could harm expression and lawful use for everyone. articles.content: We submitted our counter comments to the TRAI yesterday, on the issue of Network Slicing, which appeared as being buried by the regulator in an innocuous Quality of Service consultation.  Download: Our submission here . The zip file contains both the PDF, and a .md file you can give you AI to query our submission Network slicing is a feature of 5G networks, wherein a single network can be sliced into multiple virtual slices, and each slice an operate differentially from the other: it can, like Airtel has done, be sliced by type of customer, such that a better quality of service is provided to postpaid customers, or it can be sliced by application/service/content wherein better speeds, lower latency, congestion priority can be provided for accessing a specific service.  Reliance Jio and the telecom industry body GSMA, in their consultation submission, made arguments that when seen together suggest that Network Slicing is already unrestricted under telecom regulations, and that application/service/content specific network slices are already permitted or should be permitted.  In our submission to TRAI we’ve made the following points, which, I’ll be honest, are the exact same arguments I’ve made in favour for Net Neutrality over the last 13-14 years. The more things change, the more they remain the same. Here are key excerpts from the submission: The neutrality expected of the networks also apply to slices of the network India’s rules around differential pricing and network neutrality are applicable to the technology of network slicing as well: slices cannot be used to discriminate between applications/services/content on the basis of speed, latency, reliability, packet loss, congestion priority and price. As a country, we cannot allow telecom operators to manipulate what consumers consume on the Internet by instituting anti-neutrality practices, just as network slicing based on speed, latency, reliability, packet loss, congestion priority and price. Telecom operators don’t own the spectrum: it is licensed to them in public interest, and regulations exist to ensure non-discriminatory behaviour. There is no set of principles as core to the functioning of the Internet as those of Net Neutrality, and the freedom that users have to view and consume content and services, without the service provider influencing or interfering with their choice. How the network is sliced can be an issue Network slicing is by itself is not violative of Net Neutrality, but how the network is sliced can be an issue: it can be neutral and enable access to all services equally in a slice, or it can violate net neutrality by offering application specific slicing and service-level slicing in different slices, and additionally, price different slices differentially. 3. What cannot be done directly, cannot also be done indirectly Thus any provision for specialised services shouldn’t be allowed to be used to circumvent regulations related to prioritization or zero rating. Internet Access Providers must also be prevented from charging services any additional money for preferential treatment, to ensure that an incentive structure isn’t created for more services opting to become “specialised services”. In its February 2016 prohibition of discriminatory tariffs for data services regulations, the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India ruled that: “Further, applying the principle that what cannot be done directly, cannot also be done indirectly, TSPs are also prohibited from entering into arrangements that have the same effect as charging discriminatory tariffs on the basis of content.” We believe the same principle of “what cannot be done directly, cannot also be done indirectly” must also apply in case of specialised services. 4. Net Neutrality is essentially about three principles All sites and apps must be equally accessible: ISPs and telecom operators should not block certain apps and sites, just because they don’t pay them a revenue share. No gateways to the Internet should be allowed, and no preferential listing of certain sites, whether via commercial arrangements or not. All sites must be accessible at the same speed (at an ISP level): This means no speeding up of certain sites because of business deals. More importantly, it means no slowing down some sites. The cost of access must be the same for all sites (per Kb/Mb or as per data plan): This means no “Zero Rating”, or differential rating for different sites, apps or services. In countries like India, Net Neutrality is more about cost of Internet access than speed of Internet access, because we don’t have fast and slow lanes: all lanes are slow. 5. Telecom operators should not shape consumer choice by treating different services differentially: The Internet is not ten, hundred, ten thousand or even a million websites. It comprises hundreds of millions of sites and applications, which are available to all Internet users to choose from. This has been made possible because the access service provider does not influence consumer choice by either modifying the speed of Internet access, availability of sites and services and price of accessing a particular website or service. We would urge you to ensure that the petty self-interest of oligopolistic telecom operators and large Internet companies does not hold innovation, freedom of expression, access to information and knowledge to ransom. A structure needs to be put into place to ensure that providers of Internet access (telecom operators and ISPs) are not in a position to influence which site or service on the Internet consumers prefer to access: that choice must be of the consumer’s alone. For innovation to take place, platforms have to be affordable, stable and neutral. 6. There’s precedence of telecom operators manipulating access quality by service On the Internet, every millisecond matters. Websites in the past have shown an increase in performance after shaving milliseconds off their loading time. Traffic management may be misused as follows: Network service providers could make some websites faster than others in exchange for money or via partnership. For example: Following a partnership with Google, for the Indian Premier League in 2010, Airtel had provided a fast lane to users accessing YouTube, increasing their speed to 2 Mbps. Network service providers could make some websites slower than others. For example, in 2014, users found that the video service Ogle was slow even on an 8mbps Airtel connection. It was alleged that Airtel was throttling Ogle. Network service providers could make their own services faster than others. For example: prior to Net Neutrality regulations, in 2015, games downloaded from Airtel’s “Games on Demand” service were available at a speed higher than that of other service providers, with download speeds for users not on a 2mbps plan upgraded while downloading games from the Airtel service, no matter which plan they have signed up for. 7. If allowed, this is how telecom operators may slice services: Video streaming services like Amazon Prime, Netflix and JioStar may be bundled into a separate video slice with higher quality of service on-demand. This will mean that in order to be able to stream a service, these services may have to pay a telecom operator for that slice since the standard slice might have poor quality of service. Alternatively, customers might be charged separately for better quality of service for streaming. This creates an incentive for the telecom operator to degrade the quality of service for video. It also gives JioStar a competitive advantage because of vertical integration with Reliance Jio. There’s a clear conflict of interest for Reliance Jio here. GSMA is anyway a representative body of telecom operators. *** Telecom operators may create a separate slice for internet telephony , and prioritise certain applications that sign up for this. There is precedence in the past, with Airtel creating a separate pack for VoIP in December 2014, charging customers separately to use VoIP. If you enable service or application specific slicing, companies like Airtel will be able to degrade or make more expensive VoIP services that are outside of these packs, or maybe offer a degraded quality of service to others. 8. Telecom operators could use network slicing to prioritise their own services It is easy for telecom operators to launch products that compete with existing online products, and degrade the experience of all other services. Therefore, it is essential, in order to maintain fair competition and diversity of availability of both content and services Zero rating own services: Bharti Airtel, when it launched its online music streaming service Wynk, waived data charges for Airtel users, using its ownership of content and carriage. This effectively puts competitors like Saavn, Gaana and Rdio at a competitive disadvantage, with no means to competing. Speeding up own services: Games downloaded from Airtel’s “Games on Demand” service are available at a speed higher than that of other service providers, with download speeds for users not on a 2mbps plan upgraded while downloading games from the Airtel service, no matter which plan they have signed up for. Blocking competing services: Vodafone and Airtel had blocked Netcore’s MyToday Mobile VAS service, since MyToday’s content over SMS competed with telecom operators vertically integrated service. There is every scope of Reliance Jio and other telecom operators prioritising their own services over others. It is easy for telecom operators to launch products that compete with existing online products, and degrade the experience of all other services. Therefore, it is essential, in order to maintain fair competition and diversity of availability of both content and services that telecom operators are restricted from adopting anti-competitive and predatory practices. 9. India rejected the idea that telecom operators should be allowed to play gatekeeper At the core of this debate is the issue of how we let one business regulate the consumers’ ability to access another, given that spectrum is not unlimited. Should better technology, and indeed, the usage of national resources like spectrum, and the future of thousands of Internet companies be forsaken to protect the interests of an oligopoly of 2 telecom operators? In enforcing Net Neutrality in 2016 via the differential pricing order, the Net Neutrality order in 2017/18 and enshrining Net Neutrality in the license conditions, India rejected the idea that telecom operators should be allowed to play gatekeeper. *** India has one of the largest populations of Internet users in the world, most of whom have come online in a relatively short period of time. At the heart of the Digital India initiative is the goal of providing Internet connectivity to all Indian citizens. It is important that while trying to make the Internet available to every Indian citizen, we are also conscious of what kind of an Internet is being made available to them. We should not compromise the basic principles of the Internet based on lobbying large telecom operators like Reliance Jio and GSMA: the Internet that we get as Indians get should be open, neutral and non-discriminatory, for it to enable collaboration, innovation and progress. The Internet Freedom of our citizens and startups was not sold to telecom operators with the spectrum auctions. We would urge you to protect Net Neutrality, and not allow telecom operators to manipulate how consumers consume content on the Internet by instituting anti-neutrality practices. There must be no manipulation of speed, availability or cost of Internet access based on the site, app or service used. 10. The Internet Freedom of our citizens and startups was not sold to telecom operators with the spectrum auctions India has one of the largest populations of Internet users in the world, most of whom have come online in a relatively short period of time. At the heart of the Digital India initiative is the goal of providing Internet connectivity to all Indian citizens. It is important that while trying to make the Internet available to every Indian citizen, we are also conscious of what kind of an Internet is being made available to them. We should not compromise the basic principles of the Internet based on lobbying large telecom operators like Reliance Jio and GSMA: the Internet that we get as Indians get should be open, neutral and non-discriminatory, for it to enable collaboration, innovation and progress. The Internet Freedom of our citizens and startups was not sold to telecom operators with the spectrum auctions. *** The Internet is a space without precedence, in that it is uniquely non-discriminatory. A non-discriminatory Internet decentralizes the sources of innovation because everyone can create Internet services and applications without having to obtain permission from telecom companies. It allows collaborators to create open source and free tools to provide an alternative to proprietary tools, and improve on them. Today, a text messaging platform, Whatsapp, can incorporate voice calling over Internet protocol without needing permission. Line has incorporated messaging, calling and games into a single application. WeChat has done this and added e-commerce. There are games that integrate messaging and Internet Telephony, allowing gamers to interact with each other while playing. Everything is a remix on the Internet. All businesses are about bundling and unbundling, and there is no ecosystem in existence that is as agile, innovative, free and competitive as the Internet. 11. Startups need low friction, predictable systems India’s startup ecosystem is highly competitive and increasingly global. Startups need low friction, predictable systems where startups can operate without having to negotiate agreements with telecom operators for connectivity or speed. If you allow service/application/content specific slicing, you will facilitate the creation of impediments which will force Internet businesses from India to seek to operate in markets that offer more freedom than ours. In a global economy where countries compete to attract the best businesses, talent and investment, you will leave India worse off if you don’t protect Net Neutrality, and prevent service/application specific Network Slicing. The lack of revenue-sharing agreements with telecommunications operators, such as network usage fees, facilitates a more level playing field. Startups, including those in their initial stages, can develop their businesses without concern that internet service providers will favor competitors with more substantial financial resources. 12. It enables telecom operators to become kingmakers , and enable concentration of power with telecom operators and large Internet companies: Concentration of power with large companies: Large companies like Google and Facebook, both of which have previously inked anti-net neutrality agreements with telecom operators will benefit at the cost of upstart competitors. Remember that an Indian company, Zoho competes with Google Docs. Imagine if it cost more to access Zoho than Google Docs, because of a collusive agreement between Google and Airtel. In AI, OpenAI and Anthropic may partner with Reliance Jio, but an Indian company like Sarvam may not. It would hurt Sarvam if its AI responds more slowly than ChatGPT and Anthropic, or Jio’s own AI service. As a reminder: telecom operators are not neutral by nature. In 2008, Airtel and Vodafone had blocked Netcore’s MyToday services for no apparent reason. ** Telecom operators are meant to be pipes: mere access service providers neutral to the content that the user is accessing. This converts them into MSO’s, and allows them to choose which service or package of services gets accessed, at what speed and at price. Concentration of power with telecom operators: It enables telecom operators to become kingmakers. We’ve seen this play out in Mobile VAS, where telecom operators would gatekeep access to services for customers, and take a revenue share. 13. The TRAI should examine its own role and not allow telecom operators to become the Land Mafia of the Internet Zoom out and examine your role in the context of the future for this country, which holds the potential for the creation of thousands of Zomatos, Flipkarts, Zeptos, Shiprockets, Paytms, and whether changing the rules of Internet access hampers or spurs innovation. Steps must be taken to ensure that telecom operators don’t operate like the Land Mafia of the technology space. A government policy that actively permits predatory behavior is either indicative of a scam, or the recipe for many. articles.title: UN AI Agenda Needs Human Rights Recentering
articles.content: September 21 @ 9:00 am – 10:30 am EDT Hybrid side event during UNGA81 High-Level Week In-person attendance available upon request: email [email protected] join the livestream Add to Calendar Google Apple Outlook 365 Outlook Live Panelists: Louise Lund Henneberg , Acting Director/Techplomacy, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Denmark Wafa Ben Hassine , Chief, Digital Technology and Human Rights Section, Rule of Law, Accountability and Civic Space, Oﬀice of the High Commissioner for Human Rights Beatriz Busaniche , Executive Director, Fundación Vía Libre Luda Svystunova , Head of Social Research, Amundi Moderator: Alejandro Mayoral Baños , Co-Executive Director, Access Now During the first session of the Global Dialogue on AI Governance, governments and stakeholders convened to have open, transparent and inclusive discussions on artificial intelligence governance. We now gather experts across the spectrum of stakeholders during UNGA81 to reaffirm that human rights should be the stepping stone of this process, instead of an afterthought. None of this is irreversible, but the security issues associated with advanced AI tools are the consequences of deliberately prioritizing profit and competitiveness over the security and safety of at-risk communities, and they will not resolve on their own. Unbridled AI adoption combined with unacceptably lax corporate security practices demands urgent intervention at all levels, starting from putting human rights back at the center of digital governance mechanisms. This discussion has the objective to explore concrete, actionable ways in which each stakeholder can contribute to oppose the normalization of surveillance. Experts will also discuss how to chart a way forward to reaffirm digital rights as the natural first line of defense against the abuses of AI technologies. Hosted by: Co-sponsor:
articles.summary: A growing chorus of experts is calling for the United Nations' AI governance agenda to be recentered around human rights, shifting focus from surveillance concerns to fundamental freedoms. This push aims to ensure that international AI policies prioritize individual dignity and prevent algorithmic discrimination, censorship, and mass surveillance. The debate highlights the critical juncture at which global AI regulation stands, where foundational values must be established before technological capabilities outpace ethical safeguards.

articles.content: 본문 IT 테슬라·딥시크, 국내 이용자에 영어·중국어 회신…개인정보위, 개선 권고 강재구 기자 수정 2026-09-16 18:38 펼침 0:00 Your browser does not support the audio element. 송경희 개인정보보호위원회 위원장이 지난 9일 수요일 정부서울청사에서 제19회 전체회의를 개최하며 모두발언을 하고 있다. 개인정보보호위원회 제공 개인정보보호위원회가 국내 이용자의 개인정보 관련 문의에 외국어로 답하거나 회신하지 않은 5개 사업자에 개선을 권고했다. 개인정보위는 지난 9일 전체회의를 열고 이같은 내용을 심의·의결했다고 16일 밝혔다. 관련 내용을 보면, 테슬라코리아와 딥시크는 국내 이용자의 개인정보 관련 문의에 각각 영어와 중국어로 회신한 것으로 드러났다. 인공지능 서비스 기업 뤼튼테크놀로지스는 이용자의 권리행사 문의에 회신하지 않은 것으로 파악됐다. 개인정보위는 이들 3개 사업자에 국내 정보주체의 권리행사 요구가 원활히 접수 및 처리되도록 운영체계를 개선할 것을 권고했다. 국내 대리인 운영과 관련해 오픈에이아이(AI)와 나이키는 국내 이용자가 전화로 문의했을 당시엔 별도 이메일 창구를 안내했으나, 해당 이메일로 접수된 문의에는 회신하지 않은 것으로 확인됐다. 개인정보위는 두 사업자에 국내 대리인을 통해 개인정보 관련 고충과 상담이 원활히 처리되도록 관리·감독 강화를 권고했다. 개인정보위는 지난해 개인정보 처리방침 평가를 진행한 뒤 ‘미흡’ 평가를 받은 기업에 결과를 통보했다. 이어 신청 기업을 대상으로 전문위원이 직접 사업장을 찾아 맞춤형 현장 지원을 진행하고 이행 여부를 확인했다. 점검 결과 대체로 개선이 이뤄졌으나 일부 기업에선 추가 보완이 필요하다고 판단해 권고에 나섰다. 고낙준 개인정보위 예방조정심의관은 “정보주체의 원활한 권리행사를 저해하는 사항에 대해서도 지속적으로 점검·개선해 나가겠다”고 말했다. 강재구 기자 j9@hani.co.kr
